candidates.text: We optimized our hiring funnel so much that we started rejecting great engineers for bad whiteboard days. Took us two years to notice the pattern.
Hiring measures interview performance more than job performance. The best candidate I ever worked with failed three loops before someone took a chance on him.
Most interview processes end up selecting for people who are good at interviews. Actual job skills are almost an afterthought once the process gets big enough.
The signals companies use to hire have almost nothing to do with the work. Everyone knows it, and the process stays the same anyway.

picked: We optimized our hiring funnel so much that we started rejecting great engineers for bad whiteboard days. Took us two years to notice the pattern.

candidates.text: Every founder I know complains about the talent shortage while offering 80 percent of market rate. The shortage is not of talent, it is of people willing to be underpaid.
A lot of companies are not really hiring, they are lottery hunting. They want senior output at junior pay and genuinely believe the right person is out there desperate enough to take it.
Hiring managers all think they will be the one to find the undervalued genius. Meanwhile the actual good candidates get three offers in a week and never see their posting.
The fantasy of the cheap rockstar dies hard. Most companies would rather wait six months for a bargain than pay market rate for someone good who is available now.

picked: A lot of companies are not really hiring, they are lottery hunting. They want senior output at junior pay and genuinely believe the right person is out there desperate enough to take it.

candidates.text: The honest answer about why most startups fail is that nobody knows, including the founders. I shut down my first company in 2019 and I still could not tell you if it was the market or our execution. Probably both, in proportions I will never measure.

Postmortems rarely capture the real reason a startup dies. Was it the market, the timing, the team, the pricing? Even the founders are usually guessing, because the signals all arrive mixed together and nobody wants to write the honest version anyway.

In my experience most failed startups never get a real diagnosis. Sales were slow, but was that the product, the pitch, or the market? The team moves on, everyone picks the lesson that flatters them, and the next venture repeats it.

Failure analysis in startups is mostly storytelling. You ran out of money, sure, but why? Product, market, team, timing. Every retrospective picks one and ignores the rest, because the real answer is usually all four at once.

picked: The honest answer about why most startups fail is that nobody knows, including the founders. I shut down my first company in 2019 and I still could not tell you if it was the market or our execution. Probably both, in proportions I will never measure.

candidates.text: Every failed startup produces the same Medium post. Long on feelings, short on numbers. Then the founder either raises again on the strength of the lesson or disappears into a big company for five years.
Startup postmortems are a genre now. Three thousand words about resilience and gratitude, two sentences about why revenue never showed up. Then a pivot to advising.
The postmortem always says we ran out of runway. It never says we built something nobody wanted for eighteen months straight. Then comes the next deck.
Reading startup postmortems you would think failure is a spa retreat. Lots of growth, lots of gratitude, zero unit economics. Six months later the same person is a VP somewhere.

picked: Every failed startup produces the same Medium post. Long on feelings, short on numbers. Then the founder either raises again on the strength of the lesson or disappears into a big company for five years.

candidates.text: After my startup went under I realized my technical skills had gone soft from two years of doing everything except coding. Spent six months grinding through projects before anyone would hire me. Thinking about trying again in a few years.

Shutting down my company left me weirdly unemployable. Too senior for junior roles, too rusty for senior ones. I did contract work for a year to rebuild, then joined a mid-size team. The itch to start something again never really left.

My startup failed in 2018 and the hardest part was admitting my engineering had fallen behind. I took a regular dev job, learned the modern stack properly, and told myself I would try again once the skills caught up. Still telling myself that.
When we folded I had founder on my resume and junior-level chops. Humbling combo. Ended up at an agency for two years just shipping, which fixed the chops if not the ego.

picked: After my startup went under I realized my technical skills had gone soft from two years of doing everything except coding. Spent six months grinding through projects before anyone would hire me. Thinking about trying again in a few years.

candidates.text: This is how headcount reduction usually happens in practice. No announcement, just a hiring freeze and goals that quietly tighten until people leave on their own. The best ones always have options first.
Quiet attrition is the oldest trick in the book. Make the targets uncomfortable, stop backfilling, and let resignations do the work a layoff would. Cheaper, quieter, and no press release required.
Companies figured out a while ago that a formal layoff is the expensive way to shrink. Freeze hiring, raise the bar on reviews, and the org chart deflates on its own within two quarters.
There is a reason CFOs love attrition plans. No severance, no headlines, no morale crater. Just a slow leak that looks like natural turnover until you chart it.

picked: This is how headcount reduction usually happens in practice. No announcement, just a hiring freeze and goals that quietly tighten until people leave on their own. The best ones always have options first.

candidates.text: People assume the laid off colleagues got the worst of it. Mine mostly landed within a quarter, severance in hand. Those of us left behind absorbed their work and got a pizza budget for it.

I have been on both sides of a layoff round. The strange thing nobody tells you is that the survivors often struggle more, because the work of three people lands on your desk and the guilt sits next to it.

Surviving a layoff is its own kind of bad outcome. You keep the salary but lose the team, the roadmap, and any illusion of stability. Last time it happened to me I started interviewing within a month anyway.
After our layoff round the people who stayed were arguably worse off. Same pay, double the load, and a calendar full of meetings about reprioritization. Half of us left within a year anyway.

picked: People assume the laid off colleagues got the worst of it. Mine mostly landed within a quarter, severance in hand. Those of us left behind absorbed their work and got a pizza budget for it.

candidates.text: We cut all recurring meetings for a quarter as an experiment. Alignment collapsed within a month. The answer was never zero meetings, it was fewer, shorter ones with an actual agenda.

The meeting debate always frames it as meetings versus no meetings, when the real problem is bad meetings. A fifteen minute standup with a clear owner beats a week of scattered Slack threads every time.
Meetings are like any tool, useless when misused. Our team keeps two rules: default to twenty minutes, and anyone can leave when their part is done. Complaints dropped to almost zero.
I worked at a place that banned meetings on Wednesdays. People just crammed five hours of calls into Tuesday and Thursday. The calendar was not the problem, the culture was.

picked: I worked at a place that banned meetings on Wednesdays. People just crammed five hours of calls into Tuesday and Thursday. The calendar was not the problem, the culture was.

candidates.text: Burnout advice fails because it treats one disease with many causes. Mine was not overwork, it was working on things I did not believe in. No amount of yoga fixes that.

Every burnout thread has the same fifty contradictory answers because the fix depends entirely on what is draining you. For some people it is rest, for others it is quitting, for others it is just a different manager.
The reason burnout advice is so inconsistent is that it is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Sometimes the cure is a vacation. Sometimes it is a new career. Same feeling, different problem.
I read every burnout article for a year and none of them helped, because mine came from boredom, not exhaustion. Generic advice assumes everyone is tired in the same way.

picked: Burnout advice fails because it treats one disease with many causes. Mine was not overwork, it was working on things I did not believe in. No amount of yoga fixes that.

candidates.text: Started my son on Python at 9 and the only real problem is he now thinks indentation errors are a personal attack. Pick whatever gets them building something they care about fastest.
Teaching my daughter Scratch first and Python second. The language matters less than I thought, what matters is that she gets the win of making something work quickly enough to stay hooked.
We overthink the first language question. Kids need fast feedback and visible results. Python or Scratch gets them there, and the concepts transfer to whatever they learn next anyway.
The first language debate is mostly for adults. My kid does not care about type systems, she cares that her game character jumps when she presses space. Python does that fine.

picked: Started my son on Python at 9 and the only real problem is he now thinks indentation errors are a personal attack. Pick whatever gets them building something they care about fastest.

candidates.text: I have been the engineer assigned to open source a dying internal project. The goal was never adoption, it was a soft landing for the code and a press line for the blog. Real commitment looks different.

Corporate open source is often just a graceful exit for projects the company no longer wants to fund. Release the code, collect the goodwill, quietly reassign the team. The tell is whether maintainers stay employed on it.
Watch what companies open source versus what they keep. It is almost never the crown jewels. It is the internal tool they stopped investing in, gift wrapped as community contribution.
Open sourcing a project costs nothing when you have already stopped paying for it. The meaningful signal is headcount. If no full time maintainer is attached, it is an obituary, not a gift.

picked: I have been the engineer assigned to open source a dying internal project. The goal was never adoption, it was a soft landing for the code and a press line for the blog. Real commitment looks different.

candidates.text: If offering a hosted version of an open tool is milking it, then every cloud company is guilty. The license allows it explicitly. That is the deal the maintainers signed up for.
Building a business on open source is the point of the license. Git became infrastructure precisely because anyone could build on it without asking permission first.
Calling it milking assumes the project loses something when others build on it. Usually the opposite happens. More users, more contributors, more reason for the project to exist.
The license is the license. If building on top of free code is exploitation, then the problem is the license choice, not the company that followed the rules.

picked: If offering a hosted version of an open tool is milking it, then every cloud company is guilty. The license allows it explicitly. That is the deal the maintainers signed up for.

candidates.text: After eight months working from home I could not tell where work ended and life began, so I tried a coworking space. Hated the noise, loved the commute ritual. Now I split the week, three days home, two there.

Did the home office thing for two years and slowly turned into someone who answers email from bed at 11pm. Rented a small office last spring and the separation fixed more than my productivity. Evenings exist again.

The coworking versus home office debate misses the real variable, which is whether your home has a door you can close. I worked from our kitchen table for a year and it nearly ended my freelance career.
I went the opposite direction. Coworking space for a year, then back home. Turns out I do not need collaboration, I need silence and a good chair. Know which animal you are before signing a lease.

picked: After eight months working from home I could not tell where work ended and life began, so I tried a coworking space. Hated the noise, loved the commute ritual. Now I split the week, three days home, two there.

candidates.text: Coworking spaces sell community but deliver wifi. I spent a year in one and made exactly two work friends, both because we kept getting the same terrible coffee machine at the same time.

Same experience here. Everyone at my coworking space has headphones on permanently, which is the universal do not disturb sign. The community the brochure promises exists mostly at the organized events, not day to day.
The paradox of coworking is that everyone goes there to be around people and then works hard to not talk to anyone. Took me months to realize the kitchen was where the actual networking happened.
I met my co-founder at a coworking space, so I am biased, but it was not organic. The space ran forced-intro lunches every Friday. Without that structure it was just strangers typing near each other.

picked: Coworking spaces sell community but deliver wifi. I spent a year in one and made exactly two work friends, both because we kept getting the same terrible coffee machine at the same time.
